item.title: A semi-infinite hydraulic fracture propagating in a poroelastic medium
item.description: arXiv:2610.14049v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We solve the near-tip coupled hydromechanical problem of a hydraulic fracture propagating in a permeable poroelastic medium, represented locally as a semi-infinite crack moving at constant velocity. In the moving tip frame, all fracture fields are steady. The porous solid obeys linear poroelasticity, fracture propagation follows LEFM, fluid flow within the tensile fracture is governed by lubrication theory, and the fracturing and pore fluids are treated as identical Newtonian liquids. The primary unknowns are the fracture opening and the fluid displacement function along the fracture, determined from the resulting non-linear system of equations. In a viscosity--toughness scaling, the problem depends on four dimensionless parameters: a dimensionless permeability $\varrho$ (associated with the intensity of fluid leak-in), a dimensionless effective confining stress $\Sigma_0'$ (measuring the relative importance of fluid leak-off and leak-in), the drained--undrained Poisson's ratio contrast $\beta$, and the poroelastic stress coefficient $\eta$. The solution evolves from a drained, toughness-dominated near-tip asymptote with uniform net pressure to an undrained, storage-viscosity-dominated far-field asymptote. Numerical solutions are obtained over parameter ranges representative of various rock types. The fully coupled model is compared with simplified models, namely uncoupled and one-way coupled formulations, over distances from the fracture front spanning laboratory-to-field scales. The resulting relative difference maps in the $(\varrho,\Sigma_0')$ parameter space identify four characteristic regimes: negligible poroelastic effects, dominance of the direct mechanical poroelastic response, importance of the poroelastic backstress, and a fully coupled regime. The latter occurs mainly at large $\varrho$ and small $\Sigma_0'$, corresponding to strong leak-in relative to leak-off.
item.dc:creator: Evgenii Kanin, Andreas M\"ori, Dmitry Garagash, Brice Lecampion

item.title: CFD Forge: A Physics-Constrained Agentic Framework for Autonomous CFD
item.description: arXiv:2610.14104v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Setting up, running, and assessing a computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulation requires substantial manual effort, from meshing and solver setup to diagnosis and interpretation, and repeating it across design variants slows engineering iteration. We present CFD Forge, an agentic framework built around OpenFOAM that carries an engineering request through case construction, meshing, solver execution, diagnostics, and reporting. A large language model interprets the request, reads the simulation evidence, identifies likely causes of problems, and proposes actions from a closed set. Automation is only useful if its results can be trusted, so acceptance is not left to the model: deterministic checks, registered for each type of flow, measure explicit criteria and decide. We demonstrate the framework on a converging-diverging nozzle and a two-dimensional forward-facing step, including geometry and operating changes requested in text. A turbulent cube, run outside the agent loop, shows why the checks matter: the solver completed and the mean drag settled, but the lateral-force oscillations were still growing, so a retrospective assessment withheld acceptance. To test this separation, we replayed 36 recorded simulation states, some with deliberately altered diagnostics, through the same model in two setups. Judging from the evidence without the check results, the model accepted 12 of the 13 detectable faults in all three repeats; with CFD Forge's checks deciding, none was accepted. The two setups also differ in prompting, and a fixed rule reached the same verdicts, so the model's value lies in the open-ended work rather than the verdict. Case files, recorded model calls, and decisions are retained for audit. A model that does the work, paired with checks that decide what is accepted, is a step toward automated CFD that can be trusted in high-throughput design and active-learning loops.

item.title: Finding a reconnection in a vortex-haystack
item.description: arXiv:2610.14316v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Counter-rotating vortex reconnection is a topology-transforming event that leads to strong vorticity amplification and is often associated with the most irregular regions of the velocity field. Detecting such events directly in turbulent flows is a major challenge due to the ambiguity inherent in the definition of a vortex and the rapid proliferation of intense small scale vortices. We develop a novel methodology by combining two tools. The first is a local in scale, space and time regularity indicator that isolates spatio-temporal regions of interest. The second is a reconnection indicator that exploits a well-known property of vortex reconnection namely, that the enstrophy (volume integral of the square of vorticity) flows from the symmetry to the collision plane. To examine the flow of enstrophy in the correct reference frame, a new method inspired by orientational order parameters in liquid crystals is developed. We then show a proof of concept for our reconnection indicator by comparing it with diagnostic methods available in the literature. The method is validated on experimental datasets from a turbulent von K\'arm\'an flow at two different resolutions, one of which allows us to probe the flow below the Kolmogorov scale, $\eta$. Our findings suggest that counter-rotating vortex reconnection could be a potential mechanism for the creation of motions at scales below $\eta$.

item.title: AI Meets Turbulence Modeling: Complex Systems Perspective
item.description: arXiv:2610.14355v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Despite widespread enthusiasm, applying artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) to turbulence modeling has yielded only modest progress, primarily due to a lack of situation-aware deployment. Data-driven Reynolds-averaged Navier--Stokes (ML-RANS) closures frequently fail to generalize across diverse flow regimes, while scale-resolving simulations (SRS) remain computationally prohibitive. As a result, ML-RANS is often misapplied outside its domain of validity, and ML-SRS is unnecessarily deployed on flows fully amenable to RANS. To guide optimal AI/ML deployment, we propose a turbulence taxonomy map parameterized by degrees of freedom ($Re$) and the degree of non-equilibrium ($SK/\epsilon$). By applying Weaver's well-recognized complexity framework, we classify turbulence into distinct physical regimes. This categorization identifies where local ML-RANS surrogates can generalize, clarifies where explicit scale resolution is physically mandatory, and highlights where physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) are most effective. Ultimately, this perspective establishes a physics-grounded framework for the flow-aware, successful deployment of AI/ML in turbulence.
item.dc:creator: Sharath S. Girimaji

item.title: Surfactant-induced Marangoni stresses and surface viscosity in Faraday instability
item.description: arXiv:2610.14983v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate the influence of insoluble-surfactant elasticity and Boussinesq-Scriven surface viscosity on the parametric instability of an interface separating two viscous fluids. The two-fluid Floquet formulation of Kumar& Tuckerman (J. Fluid Mech., vol. 279, 1994, pp. 49-68) is extended to include surfactant transport, Marangoni stresses and surface viscosity. For the parameter range considered, both mechanisms increase the onset acceleration relative to the clean interface state, but through distinct responses: Marangoni elasticity produces a non-monotonic threshold, whereas surface viscosity yields a monotonic increase towards saturation. Analysis of the corresponding unforced gravity-capillary modes shows that both mechanisms modify modal damping and natural frequency. Wavenumber selection reduces the detuning from subharmonic resonance by approximately an order of magnitude relative to that evaluated at the clean interface critical wavenumber. Along the selected branches, variations in the onset acceleration closely follow those in modal damping, with residual detuning playing a secondary role. Despite their distinct interfacial stress mechanisms, both Marangoni elasticity and surface viscosity suppress tangential interfacial motion in the strong-rheology limit, approaching a common tangentially immobilized condition.
item.dc:creator: Bochang Wang, C. Ricardo Constante-Amores

item.title: Nonlinear waves and conservative transport in soluble-surfactant falling films on compliant substrates
item.description: arXiv:2610.15048v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate finite-amplitude waves in a liquid film containing a soluble surfactant as it flows down an inclined compliant substrate. The coupled motion of the liquid and a spring-backed plate is described by a conservative weighted-residual model, which also accounts for surfactant transport in the bulk and at the free surface. The reduction retains viscous terms arising from wall motion, and its pressure closure recovers fluid added mass under uniform translation. Comparison with the coupled Orr-Sommerfeld problem gives a difference of approximately $1\%$ in the peak growth rate of the film mode at $Re=25$. Nonlinear computations are then used to examine travelling states and their dependence on substrate properties and surfactant coupling. Along the prescribed stiffness-damping path, substrate displacement decreases by more than four orders of magnitude, while wave speed changes by less than $1\%$. The extrema of free-surface elevation and liquid thickness vary differently, so surface height alone does not reliably indicate film thinning over a deformable support. In the cases studied, Marangoni coupling reduces surfactant localisation and weakens the wave and substrate response. Moving-frame reconstruction reveals recirculation near the wave crest and distinguishes propagation of the deformation pattern from transverse substrate motion. The load-work budget identifies capillary pressure as the principal net source of substrate work for the two compliant supports considered. A control calculation in which stiffness is varied at fixed damping shows a substantial change in damping loss but a comparatively small change in deformation.
item.dc:creator: Sanghasri Mukhopadhyay, Asim Mukhopadhyay

item.title: Physics Foundation Models for Efficient Control of Fluid Flows
item.description: arXiv:2610.15173v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate whether a physics foundation model (PFM) pretrained for PDE forecasting can be repurposed for closed-loop fluid-flow control. We construct a PFM-based controller by attaching lightweight Gaussian actor and critic heads to frozen pretrained representations and train the policy using proximal policy optimization (PPO). We evaluate the approach on HydroGym's two-dimensional Kolmogorov-flow environment using vorticity observations at \(64\times64\) and \(128\times128\) resolutions and Reynolds numbers \(\mathrm{Re}=100\) and \(200\). Across these settings, we compare the frozen PFM controller against a baseline MLP policy trained with the same PPO framework. The PFM controller achieves consistently higher reward while requiring smaller executed action magnitudes over training, indicating improved control performance with reduced control effort. These results provide initial evidence that representations learned through self-supervised next-frame prediction can be transferred directly to closed-loop fluid flow control. Project page: https://mahindrautela.github.io/morph.
item.dc:creator: Mahindra Rautela, Shaifalee Saxena, Alexander Scheinker

item.title: Numerical Modeling of a Metallic Alloy Droplet Impact, Solidification, and Macrosegregation
item.description: arXiv:2610.15381v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For the first time, we study the effects of mass transfer on alloy droplet impact, solidification, and solute non-homogeneity or MacroSegregation (MS). For this purpose, a multi-physics model, including fully-coupled hydrodynamics of multiphase flow, wetting, conjugate heat transfer, phase change, and mass transfer, is established and validated carefully across several benchmarks. In addition, a concentration-flux-correction algorithm is proposed to conserve the solute mass within the droplet at the numerical discretization level. The validated model is subsequently used to explore the impact and solidification of an alloy droplet. The results show that accounting for mass transfer and solute transport improves the prediction of the dynamics of a solidifying splat, in a consistent manner with experimental observations, while this effect has been neglected in all previous studies. The analysis demonstrates that this improvement results from the flow sensitivity to the mushy region thickness, which is regulated by local solute concentration through the solidus and liquidus temperatures. Furthermore, analyses of the MS map identify several critical segregation regions most susceptible to defect initiation, such as cracking, including a long negatively segregated vein within the lamella, formed by the severe advective flow through the mush in the middle stages of the impact, a positively segregated region near the rim of the splat, appearing as a result of hook formation, and a major positively segregated zone at the top of the rim, which develops following the accumulation of the solute-rich melt sustained by washout from the lamella.
item.dc:creator: Ehsan Amani, Ali Moinirad

item.title: Local sensing of gas microflows using a levitated nanoparticle
item.description: arXiv:2610.15462v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Local measurements of gas flow in microscale geometries remain challenging due to the difficulty of micromechanical sensors implantation. Here, we use a levitated nanoparticle as a minimally invasive probe to map, with high spatial resolution, both the local pressure and velocity gas flow for a canonical example - a micropipe subjected to a pressure gradient. This technique enables characterization of nonequilibrium gas transport across several flow regimes, from slip flow to free-molecular flow. We directly observe the emergence of a nonlinear pressure distribution at large pressure ratios and obtain agreement with kinetic-theory predictions and Direct Simulation Monte Carlo calculations. These results introduce levitated nanoparticles as powerful and reconfigurable probes for microchannel gas sensing, with applications in microtechnology, micro-chemistry, and bioengineering.
