item.title: Identification of effective transport physics and optimal feedback control: Experimental demonstration on a 1600-fan wind generator
item.description: arXiv:2610.15547v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Distributed-input distributed-output (DIDO) systems arise in numerous engineering applications where large numbers of actuators generate spatially distributed physical fields that are monitored by distributed sensors. Developing physically interpretable models that enable real-time optimal control of these systems remains challenging because of the high dimensionality and strong spatial coupling between inputs and outputs. In this work, we propose a physics-based framework for modeling and closed-loop optimal control of DIDO systems from experimental input-output data. First, an effective partial differential equation (PDE) is selected among candidate transport models and discretized on the actuator grid to obtain a minimum-grid representation. Second, the PDE is solved in closed form, which yields an input-output operator with only four physically interpretable parameters. Third, the operator is incorporated into an iterative, constrained quadratic program that accounts for the actuator limits. The framework is demonstrated on the inner 40 x 40 section of the world's highest-resolution Fan Array Wind Generator (FAWG), comprising 1600 independently controlled fans with 36 distributed velocity measurements. The model describes the spatial interaction between the 1600 actuators and the measured velocity field with normalized mean absolute prediction errors of 11-20% for representative actuation patterns. The closed-loop controller reproduces all three prescribed two-dimensional velocity fields with a normalized mean absolute error below 2.3% in fewer than 10 iterations.
item.dc:creator: Tamir Shaqarin, Izz Al-Manasra, TianXiang Zhang, Andrea Ianiro, Stefano Discetti, Bernd R. Noack

item.title: Nanofluid transport in Taylor bubble flows
item.description: arXiv:2610.15812v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Taylor bubble flows with nanoparticle suspensions are regularly encountered in non-isothermal chemical synthesis and microfluidics. Despite this, a complete mechanistic insight into the coupled thermal and hydrodynamic interactions remains unresolved. Here, a Eulerian-Lagrangian framework has been developed to address this, capturing two-way momentum, energy exchange, and nanoparticle interactions under non-isothermal conditions. We find that Brownian motion acts in two opposing ways, enhancing local particle-fluid energy exchange yet driving a thermophoretic drift away from the heated wall that strengthens as particle diameter is reduced below 100 nm. At particle volume fractions of $\phi \sim 10^{-2}$, Taylor flow departs from the Nusselt scaling with dimensionless slug length, $\tilde{L}_s$, observed for particle-free flows. This coincides with alterations to bubble topology that co-benefit nanoparticle momentum and energy exchange with the carrier fluid. Examining both Poiseuille and Taylor flow problems, we observe contrasting, often opposing dimensionless heat transport behaviours, questioning the suitability of traditionally accepted mixture approaches. This work reveals that, in the visco-inertial regime ($Re > 500$), it is the interplay of hydrodynamic, Brownian, and interfacial forces, combined with the Taylor bubble and slug flow topology, which determine positive or negative $Nu$ outcomes. Interestingly, short-range particle forces at the liquid-gas interface work synergistically with the convective motion in the slug to alter local particle concentration and energy exchanges within downstream thin film and near-wall regions. The intensity of this convective flow was found to impact both slug and film transport phenomena, improving the redistribution of nanoparticles when $\tilde{L}_s \leq 1.6$ and with increasing $Re$.
item.dc:creator: Fahad Al-Gburi, Faysal Khaleel, Yulong Ding, Jason Stafford

item.title: Capillary-gravity wave resistance of a translating, pulsating source
item.description: arXiv:2610.15859v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A disturbance in steady rectilinear translation along a capillary-gravity interface radiates waves only above a minimum speed $c_{min}$, where it experiences a wave resistance; below this threshold it generates no waves, and the response is merely a localised deformation of the interface around the source, free of wave resistance. Modulating the source amplitude at a frequency $\Omega$ shifts the forcing to the sideband pair $kV\pm\Omega$, where $k$ is the wavenumber and $V$ is the translation speed, opening resonance conditions absent from the steady problem; radiation then sets in below the steady threshold $c_{min}$. Here we derive the mean wave resistance $\langle R\rangle$ of a line source in closed form, and show it to be strictly positive at every nonzero speed $V$: the drag-free below-threshold regime disappears for any $\Omega\neq 0$. Crossing the radiation transitions---where the group velocity matches the source speed---produces integrable resonant peaks in $\langle R\rangle$, whose exponents we derive, including at the cusp where two transition branches merge. Below threshold, where a steadily moving source feels no drag, $\langle R\rangle$ rises from zero as $\Omega^5$ (at fixed $V$). Throughout, surface tension is essential to $\langle R\rangle$: because it controls the short, dominant capillary-scale waves, discarding it misrepresents $\langle R\rangle$ over almost the entire speed-frequency plane.
item.dc:creator: Haim Diamant, Elie Raphael

item.title: Wave-driven geostrophic vortices in rotating turbulence
item.description: arXiv:2610.15863v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We perform direct numerical simulations of rotating turbulence to investigate the mechanisms responsible for the maintenance of large-scale geostrophic vortices. We confirm that the Reynolds stresses generated by inertial waves are consistent with the Reynolds-Averaged Navier-Stokes balance of the large-scale flow and demonstrate the predicted cyclone-anticyclone asymmetry, with cyclones exhibiting stronger azimuthal velocities and more compact cores. Wave-field analysis provides evidence that geostrophic vortices selectively reflect and absorb inertial waves according to the sign of their angular momentum. Wave absorption occurs either through the formation of a critical layer ahead of the reflection point or through enhanced viscous dissipation associated with increasing local wavenumber. As rotation increases, fewer inertial waves undergo resonant absorption, reducing angular-momentum transfer to the vortices and weakening the geostrophic flow. Consequently, the fraction of energy contained in geostrophic modes depends non-monotonically on the rotation rate, demonstrating that sufficiently rapid rotation can ultimately suppress, rather than enhance, turbulence two-dimensionalization.
item.dc:creator: Vladimir Parfenyev, Sergey Vergeles

item.title: Planar intrusions from a narrow, jet-like source in a linearly stratified ambient
item.description: arXiv:2610.16011v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present two and three dimensional direct numerical simulations of planar intrusions injected from a continuously supplied, narrow source into a linearly stratified ambient at the level of neutral buoyancy. The evolution passes through three phases. A laminar leading vortex dipole first advances at constant speed with a varicose wave train behind it; the trailing jet then undergoes a sinuous instability whose initial growth rate and wavelength agree with inviscid unstratified planar-jet theory evaluated on the local jet; the flow finally relaxes into a buoyancy-controlled wedge whose area grows linearly in time. Three-dimensional simulations show that the transition remains organized by the planar instability, while three-dimensionality reshapes the near-source region into a slowly evolving, actively mixing zone that entrains an additional twenty to one hundred percent of the source flux depending on source width. Rescaled with this measured effective flux, the downstream intrusion collapses reasonably well onto the similarity solution for a wide-source intrusion.
item.dc:creator: Hai Duc Vu, Murray Rudman, Anja Slim

item.title: Nonlocal generalization of the Chapman-Enskog method and hydrodynamic equations. Nonlocal vorticity transport in a turbulent medium
item.description: arXiv:2610.16014v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The results from [Fluid Dyn 61, 20 (2026)], concerning the generalized Chapman-Enskog method and a nonlocal (i.e., non-diffusive, spatially integral) viscous stress tensor in the Navier-Stokes equation, are extended to the case of arbitrary gradients of not only hydrodynamic velocity but also temperature. The resulting equations simplify the description of tangential discontinuities and separated flows. For the specific case of an incompressible medium, a nonlocal vorticity transport equation is derived that is structurally identical to the Biberman-Holstein equation for resonant radiation transport in plasmas and gases. A power-law form has been determined for the velocity distribution function of long-free-path vorticity carriers that satisfies empirical Richardson t^3 law for the mean square of relative separation of a pair of particles in a turbulent liquid or gaseous medium.
item.dc:creator: A. B. Kukushkin

item.title: A ghost-cell immersed boundary method for the shallow water equations on Cartesian grids: mass conservation and wetting and drying over variable topography
item.description: arXiv:2610.16148v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A ghost-cell immersed boundary method is proposed for the two-dimensional shallow water equations with a variable bed (topography), solved with an explicit Godunov-type finite volume scheme (unsplit second-order MUSCL, HLLC flux, hydrostatic reconstruction) on Cartesian grids. Ghost-cell methods leak mass through the wall. To find a robust and conservative treatment, eight constructions of the ghost values and a cut-cell form of the continuity equation were applied to seven test problems, which include wetting and drying on sloping beds and a laboratory dam break. In the resulting scheme, the ghost values are interpolated bilinearly at the image point; solid and dry nodes are excluded, and the weights of the remaining nodes are renormalized. Mass is conserved by solving the continuity equation in cut-cell form, while the momentum equations are left unchanged. The proposed scheme is about as accurate as the ghost-cell method without this modification and preserves a lake at rest whose shoreline crosses an immersed wall. Because only the continuity equation is modified, it avoids the treatment of the momentum equations on cut cells (wall pressure, cell merging) that a full cut-cell method requires.
item.dc:creator: Yuta Yaegashi (Independent Researcher)

item.title: Fingering instability of thin films with an inclined contact line
item.description: arXiv:2610.16380v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The fingering instability of thin-film flow is a significant obstacle to producing uniform and stable films in industrial processes. In the framework of lubrication theory, we investigate the linear stability of a gravity-driven thin film with an inclined contact line using numerical and asymptotic methods. The contact-line singularity is regularized by imposing the Greenspan slip model. As demonstrated by the results, although the contact-line inclination slightly enhances long-wavelength instability, it significantly suppresses the growth of spanwise finite-wavelength perturbations. Moreover, the most unstable wavenumber shifts toward the long-wave region as the inclination angle increases. The inclination of the contact line introduces complex eigenvalues, leading to traveling-wave modes, in contrast to the standing-wave modes observed for horizontal contact lines. We also performed asymptotic analysis in the limit of small wavenumbers, confirming the enhanced long-wave instability. The physical mechanisms underlying these stability characteristics are elucidated, revealing that the effects of contact-line inclination come from the eigenmode distortion and additional streamwise flux.
item.dc:creator: Ze-Hui Gao, Er-Qiang Li, Peng Gao

item.title: Onset condition of the ramified-jet regime: an experimental and theoretical study
item.description: arXiv:2610.16585v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This study experimentally and theoretically investigates the electrically induced transition of a gas-focused liquid jet into a rim-emitting sheet. Ultra-high-speed imaging was used to examine the effects of applied voltage, gas and liquid flow rates, and liquid properties on sheet formation and breakup. Fully developed, quasi-stable sheets formed with ethanol, whereas isopropanol exhibited only initial sheet formation. Increasing voltage promoted sheet stretching, finer and more numerous rim jets, and a narrower spray. Higher gas flow rates shifted the transition towards the nozzle and produced finer structures, while higher liquid flow rates generated larger sheets with thicker rims. A first-order theoretical model assumes an equipotential interface and neglects finite charge relaxation, hydrodynamic perturbations, and nonlinear evolution. It balances destabilizing Maxwell-pressure perturbations against restoring capillary-pressure perturbations on a conducting cylindrical jet. The model identifies the elliptic azimuthal mode, m = 2, as the first unstable mode leading to sheet formation and predicts a critical electric Bond number of 3. Predicted onset voltages agree with measurements within 20%, and the threshold was consistent with published ramified-electrospray observations. The agreement with experiments supports electrocapillary symmetry breaking as the mechanism of onset and provides a compact, physically grounded criterion for predicting the transition from electrified jets to rim-emitting sheets.
item.dc:creator: Bor Zupan, Jernej Ku\v{s}ar, Bo\v{z}idar \v{S}arler

item.title: Versatile two-layer model for thermohydraulic prediction of microchannel heat sinks
item.description: arXiv:2610.16716v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Three-dimensional conjugate heat-transfer simulations provide detailed predictions for microchannel heat sinks but can be computationally demanding when many geometries and operating conditions are evaluated. This study develops a versatile two-layer model (VTLM) that reduces the three-dimensional problem to two coupled two-dimensional fields while retaining the in-plane geometry of the flow passages and fins. Effects associated with the unresolved channel-height direction are incorporated through hydraulic and thermal closures that account for wall friction and the fluid- and fin-side contributions to interlayer heat transfer. The closures are evaluated from the representative channel geometry, flow-development condition, and fin configuration. The VTLM was assessed against three-dimensional reference models across broad ranges of channel aspect ratios and operating conditions, including uniform and nonuniform fin arrangements. Compared with the existing two-layer models, the VTLM showed improved overall agreement with the three-dimensional reference results. The results showed that prediction accuracy was governed mainly by the flow-development condition and channel aspect ratio, from which a conservative screening guideline was proposed for the examined straight-channel configurations. The assessment of finned expansion--contraction channels further supported the applicability of the VTLM to the investigated passages with abrupt width changes. Overall, the VTLM provides a reduced-dimensional framework for thermohydraulic analysis across the range of microchannel heat-sink configurations examined in this study without explicitly resolving the channel-height direction.
item.dc:creator: Chih-Hsiang Chen, Kentaro Yaji

item.title: Second-order fluids and the choice of objective derivative
item.description: arXiv:2610.16917v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We generalize the second-order fluid constitutive model to accommodate a range of possible frame indifferent time derivatives. Using the Gordon--Schowalter derivative, which contains the upper-convected, lower-convected, and corotational (Jaumann-Zaremba) derivatives as subsets, we show how the subjective choice of derivative may change model predictions and we identify features that remain universal independent of this choice. Writing these models in terms of generic coefficients is non-universal and may lead to misinterpretations of flow predictions. However, writing the models in terms of zero-shear material functions or terminal relaxation time reveals universal and robust representations.
item.dc:creator: Maxwell C. Marsh, Randy H. Ewoldt

item.title: DeboRheo v2.0: Improved Robustness for Geometrical VOF Simulations of Viscoelastic Two-Phase Flows
item.description: arXiv:2610.17082v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present DeboRheo v2.0, an unstructured, geometrically unsplit Volume-of-Fluid framework implemented in OpenFOAM for viscoelastic two-phase flows. Version 2.0 improves numerical robustness when large viscosity contrasts coincide with strongly deformed interfaces and thin viscoelastic lamellae or filaments. The revised interfacial viscosity treatment retains a sharp geometric interface while regularizing the viscous contribution to the momentum equation. The solver combines mass-momentum-consistent phase advection, optional SIMPLEC pressure-velocity coupling, and a modular rheological framework with conformation-tensor stabilization. We assess the method using two-dimensional, axisymmetric, and three-dimensional benchmarks governed by the Oldroyd-B and exponential Phan-Thien-Tanner models. The results agree well with published numerical and experimental data and demonstrate improved robustness for demanding viscoelastic free-surface configurations on unstructured meshes.
item.dc:creator: Daulet Izbassarov, Matthias Niethammer, Rahul Subburaj, Dieter Bothe, Francesco Roman\`o, Renjie Hao, Metin Muradoglu, Tomislav Maric

item.title: One vertex generates the hard-sphere Boltzmann collision hierarchy
item.description: arXiv:2610.17123v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Boltzmann equation is the fundamental kinetic bridge between molecular mechanics and fluid behaviour. It converts binary encounters into the evolution of a velocity distribution, underlies rigorous routes from hard-sphere dynamics to Euler and Navier--Stokes--Fourier equations, and remains indispensable when continuum descriptions fail, from hypersonic shock layers and atmospheric re-entry to rarefied multiscale flows. Yet its nonlinear collision term is conventionally represented by an infinite three-index tensor of collisional brackets, with apparently new coefficients at every polynomial order. Here we prove that this entire hard-sphere tensor contains only one primitive collision law: the exact rank-two stress-production vertex $S$. Every polynomial collision vertex is obtained from $S$ by a finite sequence of universal differential and tensor operations, and every conventional bracket follows by differentiation. Thus the interaction physics and its representation separate exactly: all hard-sphere-specific information is concentrated in $S$, whereas the hierarchy above it is universal algebra. A blind eighth-order test in a Mach-5 shock agrees with independent collision sampling and strongly amplifies a weak kinetic precursor. The hard-sphere hierarchy is infinite in dimension, but its primitive collision content consists of a single scalar law.
item.dc:creator: I. Karlin

item.title: Preferential concentration in a periodically forced particle-laden turbulent planar jet
item.description: arXiv:2610.17353v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Periodic forcing is common in particle-laden jets, yet its influence on turbulence and inertial-particle clustering remains poorly understood. We investigate a turbulent planar jet at two Reynolds numbers, approximately 4950 and 9900 based on nozzle height, subjected to sinusoidal forcing at a frequency three orders of magnitude below the preferred jet instability. Hot-wire anemometry and high-speed particle imaging characterise the carrier turbulence, while Voronoi tessellations quantify preferential concentration of dilute inertial droplets. Despite its low frequency and moderate amplitude, forcing substantially modifies turbulence while leaving the mean-flow development nearly unchanged. The integral scale decreases by up to $40\%$, while forced and unforced jets retain the same time-averaged relationship between the dimensionless dissipation coefficient and Taylor-scale Reynolds number. Within the forcing cycle, velocity fluctuations and the Taylor microscale vary approximately in opposite phase, keeping the Taylor-scale Reynolds number within $\pm10\%$ of its cycle mean despite substantial variations in dissipation and Kolmogorov time scale. Particle clustering is even more sensitive, with forcing increasing mean preferential concentration and producing phase-dependent variations of $21$--$49\%$ of the cycle mean. Clustering peaks when the Kolmogorov time scale is largest, corresponding to the smallest particle Stokes number. Thus, markedly different clustering states occur at similar instantaneous Taylor-scale Reynolds numbers. These findings demonstrate that weak temporal modulation can control particle organisation without substantially altering the mean transporting flow.
item.dc:creator: Mohammad Ahmad, Pierre Bragan\c{c}a, Christophe Cuvier, Martin Obligado

item.title: A complete forward projection algorithm through cylindrical and spherical refractive windows
item.description: arXiv:2610.17413v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cylindrical or spherical windows often appear in experiments and real applications. Measuring through those windows requires projecting 3D points to pixels, which is different to compute due to refraction. A point may have multiple projected images but cannot be efficiently determine with the existing projection algorithms. Using the ray's conserved momenta, we reduce this projection to closed-form equations with a concave structure. As a result, we can successfully determine whether a 3D point has a single projection or multiple and compute those locations. In simulations, with one single search, we can recover images that iterative methods miss even with many restarts. A wand calibration based on it can reach the precision limit set by image noise, enabling accurate 3D particle tracking in a swirling flow through cylinder windows. This algorithm shows how to predict visibility and multiple images through curved windows, shedding light for 3D pipe flow measurements, accurate underwater reconstruction, and many real applications.
item.dc:creator: Shijie Zhong, Shiyong Tan, Xiaosi Zhang, Yanying Li, Rui Ni

item.title: Gas radiation and the gravity limit of flicker in a co-flowing hydrogen jet diffusion flame
item.description: arXiv:2610.17595v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Although weak at normal gravity, gas radiation sets the gravity at which a co-flowing hydrogen jet diffusion flame stops flickering. Flamelet-based simulations with unity Lewis numbers, which reproduce the flicker frequency measured by femtosecond coherent anti-Stokes Raman scattering within 4%, are combined with local stability analysis. At one tenth of normal gravity, the adiabatic flame flickers, the radiating flame does not, and switching the emission off restores flicker. Radiation acts through two mechanisms that do not weaken at reduced gravity. The hot outer layer loses buoyancy in proportion to the gas residence time, and a disturbance that displaces the flame also displaces its emission, which damps the disturbance on the lean flank (displaced-emission damping). Freezing the radiative source, which removes only its response to disturbances, slows the downstream recession of the oscillation more than tenfold. Both mechanisms slow the upstream spreading of disturbances. This spreading, competing with the co-flow, sets the onset location and the critical co-flow. Without radiation, the spreading speed scales with the square root of gravity; its radiative reduction does not. At reduced gravity, the flicker limit therefore becomes a straight line relating the square root of the co-flow Froude number to a radiation number, the ratio of buoyant to radiative time scales. The calibrated line places the critical gravity for the experimental co-flow at 0.13 times normal gravity, 2.6 times the adiabatic value. It correctly predicted whether two further flames keep flickering. Beyond the limit, transient wave packets can mimic flicker throughout a short drop-tower test.
item.dc:creator: Tianfang Xie, Meng Wang

item.title: High-fidelity Three-Dimensional Flow Field Reconstruction Driven by Turbulent Fluid Dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2610.18045v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: High-fidelity three-dimensional turbulent flow fields are essential for scientific and engineering analyses, yet obtaining them through direct numerical simulation or high-resolution measurements remains expensive. Super-resolution reconstruction from coarse-grained data therefore offers a promising alternative, but remains fundamentally challenging because fine-scale structures are intrinsically three-dimensional and dynamically coupled across scales. Existing data-driven approaches still struggle to recover multiscale volumetric structures and their coherent temporal evolution. To address these limitations, we propose a turbulence-aware framework for time-resolved three-dimensional flow reconstruction. The framework couples a multiscale neural operator, designed to recover volumetric structures, with a state space model to promote temporal consistency in the reconstructed dynamics. In addition, Navier-Stokes residuals are incorporated as soft constraints to regularize the reconstruction toward physically plausible dynamics. A mixture-of-experts mechanism is also introduced to support unsupervised adaptation to unknown coarse-graining. Across evaluations on canonical turbulent systems and atmospheric reanalysis data, the proposed framework reduces reconstruction errors relative to learning-based and classical baselines, while better preserving multiscale spatial structure and coherent temporal evolution. These results validate the effectiveness of the proposed framework in reconstructing high-fidelity three-dimensional flow fields from coarse-grained data.
item.dc:creator: Hanlin Kong, Jianan Wei, Yuntian Chen, Yujia Wang, Wenguan Wang

item.title: One-way pressure-independent valves with hysteresis and chattering
item.description: arXiv:2610.18242v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a model for the one-dimensional isothermal gas flow through a valve in a pipe. The valve aims at keeping the outgoing flow in an assigned interval; moreover, its opening and closing depend on a further parameter. The model is realized by a system of two conservation laws with suitable conditions coupling the ingoing and the outgoing flow. We study the corresponding Riemann problem, where non-classical shocks show up. Although simple, the model allows to study two key oscillatory behaviors of the flow, which are due, respectively, to the chattering of the valve, especially seen in the numerical simulations, and to the stabilizing hysteresis induced by the valve operation. We characterize the states leading to chattering and show how they depend on the parameters of the model. Through several numerical simulations, we study the interplay between the two above phenomena.
item.dc:creator: Fabio Bagagiolo, Andrea Corli, Stefan Moreti, Massimiliano D. Rosini

item.title: Partially-Averaged Navier-Stokes simulation of turbulent annular Poiseulle flow
item.description: arXiv:2610.18254v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Turbulent annular Poiseulle flow is commonly encountered in various engineering applications, such as heat exchangers. The effects of the inner wall transverse curvature on the flowfield, characterised by the ratio of inner and outer radii $\eta = R_{i}/R_{o}$, have been studied previously using Direct Numerical Simulations (DNS). Scale-resolving simulations based on a Reynolds-Averaged Navier Stokes framework offer a potentially cheaper alternative to traditional Large Eddy Simulations (LES); however it is not clear if such models are able to capture the turbulence anisotropy in the turbulent annular pipe flow. In the present study, turbulent annular Poiseulle flow at $Re_{D_{h}} = 8900$ is performed with the Partially-Averaged Navier Stokes (PANS) model, a variable-resolution turbulence model that is based on the conventional RANS modelling. The ability of the PANS model to capture the effects of the transverse wall curvature is found to be comparable with DNS and other RANS-based scale-resolving approaches despite its relative simplicity and reduced computational cost.
item.dc:creator: Li-Toong Yap, Marten Klein, Heiko Schmidt

item.title: Preferential concentration of cloud droplets: Coupled effects of phase change and gravitational settling
item.description: arXiv:2610.18255v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cloud droplets respond to turbulent motion with finite inertia and settle under gravity, while condensation and evaporation change their sizes. The nonuniform accumulation of cloud droplets in turbulent flows, known as preferential concentration, has attracted sustained interest because it affects droplet collision and coalescence rates. We develop an analytical theory that quantifies the coupled effects of droplet inertia, gravitational settling, and phase change on concentration changes. Applying this theory to simulations of two-dimensional homogeneous thermal convection reveals that phase change markedly enhances preferential concentration in this flow, primarily through spatial differences in settling speed. These differences arise because droplets experience different thermodynamic histories along their trajectories and thus acquire different sizes. Droplet transport further increases this settling contribution by rearranging droplets of different sizes. Fluid deformation partly offsets this enhancement by thinning concentration structures, reducing the preferential concentration measured at a fixed spatial scale.
item.dc:creator: Zi-Mo Liao

item.title: Some generalizations of the tornado model
item.description: arXiv:2610.18663v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A possible mechanism of tornado generation is associated with the Schwarzschild criterion for convective instability. The supercooled cloud-air mixture near the axis starts to descend and, due to the super adiabatic temperature gradient, the overheated near-surface air mass rises. The complete system of equations for full model includes equations for the stream function, for the azimuthal velocity component, and for the change in density. The refined model considers rotating convection within the framework of ideal hydrodynamics. The simplest model uses a separate equation for the stream function and can be applied to the initial stage of vortex generation. Within the framework of the simplest model, an analytical solution is combined from 8 linear dependencies by height. Rotation increases due to the conservation of angular momentum. Within the framework of the refined model, some unidirectional differential rotation arises, but it depends on boundary conditions (can be local). The full model studies the tornado development as rotating convection from the very beginning to the quasi-stationary stage. Velocity components increase in a coordinated manner. Two cases are considered: a single whirlwind and a two-eyed tornado. Radial flows converge towards the central part of the tornado near the earth surface, and there is an outflow from the "wall" to the axis and to the periphery near the top of the tornado. The maximum vertical velocity component is achieved at a certain radial distance at a certain height. The maximum azimuthal velocity component is achieved in the tornado "wall". Tornado generation criteria are discussed.
item.dc:creator: S. N. Artekha

item.title: Generalized PINN-Based Inverse Estimation of Spatially Varying Heat Transfer Coefficients with Transfer Learning
item.description: arXiv:2610.14008v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This study investigates generalized boundary representations and transfer learning for physics-informed neural-network (PINN) estimation of spatially varying convective heat transfer coefficients (HTCs) in jet impingement cooling. Piecewise-linear (PWL) and neural-network boundary estimators are inferred from transient interior-temperature measurements and evaluated against CFD-CHT reference HTC profiles at Reynolds numbers of 5000, 10000 and 15000. A discrete Adjoint-FEM formulation with gradient regularization based on the $H^1$-seminorm provides an independent inverse-method comparison. Transfer learning is investigated under two source-target conditions: transfer between noise levels at the same Reynolds number, and transfer from a controlled Gaussian-profile problem to CFD-CHT-derived target problems at different Reynolds numbers. For the representative Re = 5000 target with 5% measurement noise, quadratic, PWL, and neural-network PINNs achieve relative HTC-profile errors of 5.08, 5.31 and 5.19%, respectively, while generalized representations reduce the error for the Re = 15000 target from 16.76% for the quadratic PINN to 14.41% and 14.46%. Transfer learning reduces target-training time by 57.86-81.71% for fixed-Reynolds-number transfer and by 50.59-84.94% for Gaussian-to-CHT transfer. Its effect on reconstruction accuracy is target dependent: fixed-profile PWL transfer remains within 0.30 percentage points of scratch training, whereas Gaussian-to-CHT transfer produces differences of 0.10-1.52 percentage points across targets and representations. These results demonstrate that generalized PINN representations can accommodate spatially varying HTC profiles without a prescribed quadratic form, while transfer learning can substantially reduce target-training cost for repeated inverse estimation, with the resulting reconstruction accuracy depending on source-target compatibility.
item.dc:creator: Pradipan Maitra, Jariful Hassan, Arijit Hazra

item.title: SIREN: A nonlinear Rankine-source boundary element solver for the stationary motion of a marine vehicle in calm water
item.description: arXiv:2610.14027v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: SIREN (Ship Inviscid Resistance and Elevation eNgine) is a Rankine-source panel solver for the steady wave resistance of a ship, in the tradition of Dawson's method. The free-surface condition is linearised about a base flow, and the linearisation is iterated. In the present formulation the base flow is the solution of a Neumann problem on the actual boundary: sources on the entire hull, wet and dry, and on the free surface panels, with impermeability imposed on both, so that the free surface acts as a rigid lid at the position it currently occupies. This replaces the classical double-body flow, whose image about z=0 is meaningful only for a flat surface and a hull cut at z=0, and it removes the need for desingularised free-surface panels. In the non-linear iteration the free-surface panels are moved rigidly in the vertical to the relaxed wave elevation at their centroid, the hull panels are marked wet or dry against the moved surface, and the base flow is recomputed on the moved geometry; impermeability applies to the whole hull regardless of this marking, which is used only to select which panels enter the force integral, and under-relaxation is confined to the passes where the non-linear correction accumulates without being reset. The radiation condition is imposed by a one-row upstream shift of the collocation points, and the wave resistance is obtained by pressure integration and, independently, by transverse wave-cut analysis.
item.dc:creator: Daniele Peri

item.title: acousticHelmholtzFoam: an MPI-parallel unstructured finite-volume solver for frequency-domain acoustics in heterogeneous two-phase media with perfectly matched layers
item.description: arXiv:2610.14057v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: acousticHelmholtzFoam is an OpenFOAM application that computes time-harmonic acoustic pressure fields in heterogeneous gas-liquid media on unstructured polyhedral meshes. The complex pressure is stored as real and imaginary volume fields, the material coefficients are constructed from a volume-of-fluid phase fraction with geometric face-fraction averaging, and open boundaries are truncated by Cartesian perfectly matched layers (PMLs) whose damping tensor is generated by the companion utility setPMLFields. The two coupled real-valued equations are discretized with the cell-centred finite-volume operators of OpenFOAM and assembled explicitly, including processor couplings and boundary contributions, into a distributed PETSc matrix that is solved by default with the MUMPS sparse direct solver. The solver writes pressure amplitude, complex velocity, acoustic radiation pressure and time-averaged momentum flux for acoustic-force evaluation. This paper documents the implemented equations, the case interface, the assembly and solution algorithm, the build procedure and the test infrastructure. A layered gas-liquid-PML case with an analytical solution serves as an end-to-end regression: on 8000 cells the whole-domain relative complex-pressure error is $1.197\times10^{-3}$, and serial and MPI solutions on up to eight ranks agree to within $10^{-12}$ in relative $L_2$ norm. A single-axis acoustic-levitator height sweep with constant-volume spheroidal drops demonstrates the two-phase material input and the force output, and strong- and problem-size-scaling measurements characterize the direct-solver workflow. The numerical formulation and its verification are presented in a companion paper (arXiv:2610.01593).
item.dc:creator: Chuanchao Xu, Jun Liu, Dieter Bothe, Tomislav Maric

item.title: Philip L. Roe, the British Scientist. The Cranfield Years and Beyond
item.description: arXiv:2610.14087v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Philip L. Roe, the renowned British scientist, passed away on April 26, 2026, at the age of 87, while Professor Emeritus at the University of Michigan. My association with Phil Roe began in 1984, when he joined the Cranfield Institute of Technology, UK, as Professor of Computational Fluid Dynamics, while I was a postdoctoral research fellow at the same institution. For more than four decades, his incisive ideas, physical principles and distinctive approach to research on numerical methods for solving hyperbolic partial differential equations have had a lasting influence on my own approach to research in the field. Here I recount some personal memories and anecdotes emerging from the rewarding experience of interacting with Phil during the Cranfield years and beyond. I also review, quite succinctly in places, some of the main research topics that he pursued throughout much of his academic career. These notes are intended as a modest homage to Roe's impact on the subject, as well as to his influence on the careers of generations of scientists in both academia and industry.
item.dc:creator: Eleuterio F. Toro

item.title: Generalized Constraint-Controlled Rheological Model: Two Constitutive Pathways under Sinusoidal Periodic Shear Deformation
item.description: arXiv:2610.15538v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We formulate the Generalized Constraint-Controlled Rheological Model (GCCRM) for entangled linear and long-arm-branched polymer melts under sinusoidal periodic shear deformation (SPSD), spanning the linear and strongly nonlinear regimes. Molecular architecture, conformation, chain stretch, flow-active constraints, convective constraint release, dynamic tube dilation, and activated arm retraction define a common upstream molecular state. This state feeds two time-domain constitutive pathways (a configurational stress and a dissipative internal-variable stress) which are recombined before Fourier analysis. For branched polymers, the architecture is described by an entire backbone of molecular weight $M_{bb}$ and $N_a$ long arms of molecular weight $M_a$, with a compliance-weighted representative-constitutive-cell partition. The linear limit is normalized so that the configurational moduli sum to the entanglement modulus, while dynamic tube dilation and stretch drive distinct contributions to dissipative activation. Under reduced closures, GCCRM generates a smooth nonlinear elastic response with an onset of nonlinearity, an approximately logarithmic growth regime, an architecture-dependent maximum, and distinct high-deformation asymptotes. Fourier harmonics, ELR, VLR, and Lissajous curves are treated as post-processing observables of the total stress. The framework establishes a consistent constitutive architecture whose quantitative validation requires one parameter set per material across SPSD and, prospectively, transient shear histories.
item.dc:creator: Dario Nichetti, Alessio Zaccone

item.title: Interaction of eccentricity tide and convection
item.description: arXiv:2610.16111v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Aim. We try to understand the interaction of eccentricity tide and convection in icy satellites. Method. We use the numerical calculation of rotating convection with eccentricity tide in a spherical shell. Results. We have the following results. (1) Energy scaling exponent about buoyancy force (or tidal force) decreases with increasing tidal force (or buoyancy force). (2) The combined tide-convection flow is not identical to superposition of two pure flows in respect of energy spectrum. (3) Tide controls large-scale of fluid motion but convection is important for small scale, and the mode-mode transition occurs at intermediate scales. (4) Tide suppresses heat transport efficiency. (5) Dissipation of kinetic energy scales as square of tidal force with a very weak dependence on buoyancy force, which has little impact on dissipation but suppresses the tidal influence on dissipation.
item.dc:creator: Jiachen Zheng, Xing Wei

item.title: Grand minima and intermittency in near-critical convection-driven dynamos
item.description: arXiv:2610.16314v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Context: Solar magnetism exhibits long-term variations on timescales of decades to centuries. Aims: The main aim is to study how the supercriticality of the dynamo affects the variability of magnetic fields on timescales relevant to the Sun. Methods: Three-dimensional rotating magnetohydrodynamic simulations in a spherical wedge geometry are used to produce self-consistent convection-driven dynamos. The supercriticality of the dynamo is controlled by varying the magnetic diffusivity. Results: The main result is that long-term variability of the dynamo increases with decreasing supercriticality of the dynamo and that cases nearest to the onset of dynamo action show extended grand minima-like periods of low activity. The simulations fall in three classes where the least supercritical cases show the largest variations of magnetic activity and where the flow including differential rotation is almost unaffected by the magnetic field. In the cases with the highest supercriticality the magnetic field is permanently strong and differential rotation permanently quenched, both having relatively little temporal variation. In an intermediate regime both the magnetic fields and differential rotation exhibit strong anticorrelated fluctuations. Conclusions: The occurrence of grand minima in the Sun has been conjectured to be due to a weakly supercritical dynamo. The current results support this idea and suggest that the absence of grand minima in earlier global dynamo simulations is because their large-scale dynamos were too supercritical. Furthermore, the current results suggest that the effect of the magnetic field on differential rotation is negligible if the average rms-field is less than about 2~kG.
item.dc:creator: P. J. K\"apyl\"a (University of Graz,KIS)

item.title: Probabilistic Simulation of Gas-Liquid Interfaces with Coupled Flow Matching on Spherical Harmonics
item.description: arXiv:2610.16327v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Bubbly flows involve strongly coupled bubble motion, deformation, and hydrodynamic interactions, making high-fidelity simulation computationally expensive. We propose a neural surrogate that jointly predicts bubble trajectories and interface deformation in a compact, shared representation, replacing costly mesh-resolved simulation with fast generative inference. Because two-phase flow dynamics is nonlinear and chaotic, we treat forecasting as a conditional generative problem rather than deterministic regression, predicting entire future windows in a single pass. We train and evaluate the surrogate on BubbleSH, a Front-Tracking dataset of rising deformable bubble swarms, assessing performance using trajectory, shape, and distributional metrics over kinematic, morphological, and interaction-based properties. The surrogate reproduces key flow statistics while running several orders of magnitude faster than the underlying DNS solver.
item.dc:creator: Kiet Bennema ten Brinke, Rachna Ramesh, Douwe Orij, Ivo Roghair, Vlado Menkovski

item.title: Space-Time Parallel Direct Numerical Simulation of Rayleigh-B\'enard Convection
item.description: arXiv:2610.17942v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Rayleigh-B\'enard convection (RBC) is a model for turbulent flow and challenging to simulate by direct numerical simulation (DNS). Adequate resolution of all relevant length scales requires very fine grids in space and stability restrictions can dictate small step sizes. In this paper, we investigate the use of parallel spectral deferred correction (SDC) as a high-order time-stepping method to reduce wall-clock times of direct numerical simulation of RBC. Performance results on JUSUF (CPUs) and JUPITER (GPUs) with two different codes show parallel SDC can offer some concurrency along the temporal axis plus larger maximum stable time steps. Taken together, this allows for a reduction of wall-clock time required for simulations over one free-fall time by having to compute fewer steps and being able to mitigate the higher cost per time step through temporal parallelization.
item.dc:creator: Thomas Saupe, Thibaut Lunet, Mathis Bode, Robert Speck, Sebastian G\"otschel, Daniel Ruprecht

item.title: Evolution of dense liquid marbles under light tapping
item.description: arXiv:2610.18074v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Liquid marbles interface is composed by a dense network of grains trapped by capillarity at their surface. The mix of capillarity and granular character make their interfaces remarkable, allowing non wetting, high mobility and strong robustness which are a basis for numerous applications. A canonical experiment showing out of equilibrium nature of granular material is the so called tapping experiment, where a dry granular medium under vertical vibration reorganize an evolve toward a denser final state function of the vibration amplitude In this paper we explore the out of equilibrium nature of densely covered liquid marbles by measuring their shape, compaction and stresses evolution under vertical vibration. We show that liquid marble do indeed reorganize when submitted to taps, leading to higher internal pressure and lower effective surface tension.
item.dc:creator: Amaelle Sprocq, Th\'eo Dhoudain, Alexis Duchesne, Guillaume Lagubeau

item.title: Linking Horizontal and Vertical Submesoscale Lagrangian Dynamics South of the Ibiza Channel
item.description: arXiv:2610.18145v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Fronts, eddies, jets, and meanders populate the ocean surface and play a key role in organizing transport and mixing across a wide range of scales. From a Lagrangian perspective, frontal structures are conveniently detected as surface filaments that act as barriers to horizontal transport. However, the degree to which these structures maintain coherence below the surface and the relationship between horizontal and vertical motions in their vicinity remain poorly understood. Here we analyze two such filaments in the western Mediterranean Sea, south of the Ibiza Channel, using a high-resolution ocean simulation and Lagrangian diagnostics specifically designed to characterize submesoscale transport. Backward Finite-Size Lyapunov Exponents (FSLE) computed at successive depths reveal nearly vertical, curtain-like structures extending several tens of meters into the water column, with intensity decreasing with depth. Vertical-velocity sections across the filaments show coherent downward motion aligned with the filament cores, while Lagrangian trajectories indicate rapid horizontal convergence of fluid particles accompanied by sustained downward displacement. The barrier effect of Lagrangian Coherent Structures (LCSs) is commonly associated with persistent dynamical features of large-scale flows. Here, however, we demonstrate that FSLE filaments generated by rapidly fluctuating submesoscale dynamics can also act as effective transport barriers. The results demonstrate that the surface signatures of Lagrangian filaments identified through FSLE techniques correspond to three-dimensional transport structures that regulate both lateral aggregation and vertical connectivity in the upper ocean.
item.dc:creator: Sara Cloux, Ismael Hernandez-Carrasco, Alejandro Orfila, Emilio Hernandez-Garcia, Cristobal Lopez

item.title: Embossing of Tapered, Isometric Micro-Interdigitated Flow Fields for Enhanced Desalination by Faradaic Deionization
item.description: arXiv:2610.18791v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Engineered transport architectures can improve electrolyte distribution and active-material utilization in porous electrodes, yet their implementation remains limited by fabrication methods that compromise precision, throughput, active-material preservation, or scalability. Here, an integrated embossing-calendering method is introduced to pattern Prussian blue analog (PBA) porous electrodes with embedded, micro-interdigitated flow fields (e$\mu$-IDFFs) for electrochemical desalination. This non-subtractive, roll-to-roll compatible method forms channels by controlling plastic deformation while simultaneously calendering the electrode, preserving active material and reducing patterning time by 100-fold relative to mechanical milling. Indentation experiments and a closed-form model further show that embossing requires 15-fold less force than stamping, while electrode microstructures show local densification beneath embossed channels. PBA electrodes are embossed with novel e$\mu$-IDFFs that use continuous width-tapering with isometric flow paths that promote uniform electrolyte distribution, increase rate capability, and reduce polarization. Compared with e$\mu$-IDFFs patterned using less scalable means and non-isometric flow paths, these e$\mu$-IDFFs desalinate seawater-salinity feeds near to potable levels with 1.5-fold of its thermodynamic energy efficiency and water recovery. Brackish desalination benefits similarly. Tapered, isometric e$\mu$-IDFFs and the embossing method introduced to pattern them are readily translated other electrochemical energy storage and separations systems.
item.dc:creator: Md Habibur Rahman, Sadia Afrin, Kyle C. Smith

item.title: Causal analysis of inner and outer motions in near-wall turbulence
item.description: arXiv:2404.08907v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In this work, we study the causality of near-wall inner and outer turbulent motions. The inner motions are defined as the self-sustained near-wall cycle, and the outer motions as those living in the logarithmic layer exhibiting footprints on the near-wall region. Causal inference with three typical methods is performed, \emph{i.e.} transfer entropy, information flow, and SURD (synergistic--unique--redundant decomposition of causality). The causal inference methods are first applied to several canonical problems to illustrate their abilities, including a linear problem, a non-linear problem, and a low-dimensional model of near-wall turbulence. It is demonstrated that all three methods can produce consistent causal findings. Furthermore, we study the causalities between the inner and outer turbulent motions in a channel flow using the three methods with an improved inner-outer decomposition method. It is revealed that both the inner and outer motions are causally self-sustained, supporting the self-sustaining mechanism of turbulent motions at all scales. We also find that there are top-down and bottom-up causalities between the outer motions and their near-wall footprints owing to the dynamical coherence of inclined large-scale turbulent motions. More interestingly, pressure is identified to play an active role in the inner-outer causalities and may act as a bridge in linking the inner and outer turbulent motions.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Journal of Fluid Mechanics, 2026, vol. 1043, A18
item.dc:creator: Jingxuan Zhang, Zhengping Zhu, Limin Wang, Wei Gao, Ruifeng Hu

item.title: Taylor dispersion and large-deviation structure in stagnation-point flows without homogenisation
item.description: arXiv:2508.17982v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study the long-time dispersion of a passive scalar in linearly accelerating flows whose strain rate $v(\eta)$ varies transversely: the axially strained flow in a porous tube with wall injection, and radially strained stagnation-point flows over a wall (Homann and von K\'arm\'an flows). Exponential stretching outpaces cross-sectional diffusion, so the scalar never homogenises across the section and classical cross-sectional averaging fails. Instead, in the logarithm of the stretched coordinate the problem becomes a Taylor dispersion problem, with mean log-stretching rate $U=\Lambda'(0)$ and log-space diffusivity $D=\tfrac{1}{2}\Lambda''(0)$: Taylor dispersion emerges without homogenisation, and only because the strain varies transversely. A Mellin-transform analysis, based on the principal eigenvalue $\Lambda(q)$ of the transverse advection-diffusion operator augmented by $qv$, gives the large-time structure in terms of the log-speed $x=\ln|\boldsymbol\xi|/t$, where $\boldsymbol\xi\in \mathbb R^d$ denotes the stretching directions ($d=1$ axial and $d=2$ radial). Essentially all the scalar mass lies in a log-normal bulk at $x=U$, flanked by forward and rear large-deviation tails with mass density $e^{-I(x)t}$, where $I(x)$ is the rate function (i.e., the Legendre transform of $\Lambda(q)$) Behind the rear tail, below $x_*=\Lambda'(-d)<U$, a plateau independent of $\boldsymbol\xi$ decays at the rate $-\Lambda(-d)$. It carries the highest concentrations but only a fraction $e^{-I(x_*)t}$ of the mass. A thin transition zone joins the plateau to the rear tail. For uniformly strained flows, as in the Burgers vortex, all regions collapse onto a single Gaussian.
item.dc:creator: Prabakaran Rajamanickam

item.title: The Weakly-Nonlinear Admittance at Open Ends of Two- and Three-Dimensional Acoustic Waveguides
item.description: arXiv:2509.21615v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We formulate a weakly-nonlinear exit condition for open ends of acoustic waveguides; to our knowledge this is the first time a general acoustic open end has been analysed outside the linear regime. The formulation neglects mean flow, vortex separation, and viscous effects. The resulting admittance boundary condition, and its weakly-nonlinear counterpart, extend recent weakly-nonlinear modelling of curved ducts (Jensen & Brambley 2026, arXiv:2503.11536) to include open ends. We approximate free space by considering the open-ended duct to be enclosed within a much larger hard-walled concentric duct; within the larger duct, the smaller duct exit is modelled as an acoustic discontinuity. Importantly, the superposition principle is unneeded, allowing the model to be applied in the nonlinear regime. The exit condition can be calculated without needing to solve the full problem in either the outer or inner ducts, making it numerically efficient. The exit condition is validated in the linear regime by comparison to Wiener-Hopf solutions of the duct end correction, and a novel nonlinear end correction is proposed; we find that both non-plane waves and nonlinearity cause the end correction to vary significantly from Rayleigh's classical 0.6 radii result. A number of numerical illustrations are then discussed, demonstrating nonlinear effects, sound radiating from curved ducts, sound radiating from an exponential horn (representative of brass instrument bells), and the harmonic effects of the open end on in-duct resonances. The model has potential applications to sound in woodwind and brass instruments. Matlab source code is provided in the supplementary material.
item.dc:creator: Freddie Jensen, Harry Turnbull, Edward James Brambley

item.title: Generalized Formulation to Predict Rossiter Modes for Subsonic to Hypersonic Flow
item.description: arXiv:2601.09099v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper describes the development of a generalized, physics-based theoretical model for estimating Rossiter modes for flow over rectangular cavities for regimes ranging from subsonic to hypersonic without requiring a priori knowledge of the detailed cavity-flow dynamics. This model addresses the issues with the Heller Bliss model, which despite incorporating compressibility effects, shows increasing deviations from experimentally measured Rossiter modes above Mach 3. The proposed model exploits the fact that the acoustic propagation speed governing the Rossiter feedback mechanism depends on the excitation and relaxation of internal energy modes. To account for these effects, an effective temperature is constructed from estimated post-shock conditions and used to evaluate an effective speed of sound, which is then used in the Rossiter relation to calculate the Strouhal number. The Strouhal numbers predicted by the model are compared with available experimental and high-resolution two-dimensional numerical simulations (conducted as a part of this study) from Mach 2 to Mach 9; our results agree very well with these datasets, thus supporting the conclusion that thermodynamic energy-mode participation and relaxation can alter the acoustic feedback timescale governing cavity oscillations. The formulation therefore provides a physics-based estimate of Rossiter-mode frequencies without requiring prior CFD or experimental characterization of the detailed cavity-flow dynamics.
item.dc:creator: Jeremy P. Redding, Luis Bravo, Prashant Khare

item.title: Aggregation, breakup, and size-dependent transport in a turbulent channel flow with cohesive particles
item.description: arXiv:2604.20028v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Due to attractive inter-particle forces, cohesive particles suspended in turbulence undergo a complex process of aggregation, breakup, and restructuring. Despite a growing body of knowledge on the ``flocculation'' of cohesive granular materials suspended in homogeneous isotropic turbulence, little focus has so far been placed on wall-bounded flows where turbulence and shear are inhomogeneous. This study presents a first investigation of a fully developed wall-bounded flow of resolved cohesive particles. Five direct numerical simulations of turbulent channel flows laden with finite-sized particles at successively increasing cohesive strength are performed. A population balance equation (PBE) framework is used to analyze aggregate dynamics. When integrated over the full domain, the PBE is closed by aggregation and breakup alone. However, this balance is found to not hold locally in the wall-normal direction, where regions of net aggregate production and depletion are identified. This imbalance is shown to be compensated by the size-dependent wall-normal transport of aggregates, revealing a mean circulation: larger aggregates are preferentially produced in the channel center and migrate toward the wall where they break, while smaller aggregates are transported away from the wall, grow, and reenter the cycle.
item.dc:creator: Alexandre D. Leonelli, Lukas Widmer, Eckart Meiburg

item.title: The rapidly advancing contact line Part-1: Navier slip and microscale inertial effects
item.description: arXiv:2605.00303v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Curtain coating, in which a moving plate is coated by a falling liquid sheet, sustains rapidly advancing contact lines at large capillary numbers Ca ~ 1. Steady-state solutions exist up to a critical capillary number, beyond which wetting failure occurs through the entrainment of air bubbles. In the steady regime, experiments report an acceleration of the velocity along the fluid-fluid interface as the contact line is approached, down to a few tens of micrometres, and this observation has been interpreted as evidence against the Navier slip model. Here we show that the observed acceleration is compatible with slip models. We perform two-phase Navier--Stokes Volume-of-Fluid simulations with quadtree adaptive mesh refinement use Navier slip and a fixed contact angle. Although the velocity vanishes at the contact line in the contact-line frame, the experimentally accessible microscale region lies outside the slip region. The local Reynolds number based on the distance from the contact line is order unity in this region, and therefore local inertial effects cannot be neglected. The scaled interfacial velocity is well described by an inertially corrected wedge flow solution whose wedge angle can be chosen as the interfacial angle at the inflection point, with agreement improving as the slip length is reduced. Reducing the slip length also recovers a non-monotonic dependence of the critical capillary number on the feed-flow Reynolds number, beyond which wetting failure occurs. At larger scales, a local Young--Laplace arc describes a finite sessile-drop-like region of the outer heel; this region contracts as the heel is suppressed.
item.dc:creator: Yash Kulkarni, Tomas Fullana, Stephane Popinet, Stephane Zaleski

item.title: Simulations of Particle-Laden Flows with Large Dispersed-Phase Size Disparities Using Scalable Parallel Adaptive Methods
item.description: arXiv:2605.20565v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The numerical simulation of multiphase flows involving dispersed components with large scale disparities, such as the collisions between millimeter-sized bubbles and micron-sized mineral particles in flotation, poses a significant computational challenge. Accurately resolving the thin boundary layers of finite-size objects while tracking massive numbers of small particles within a large turbulent domain is often prohibitively expensive on uniform grids. To address this, we present a parallel scalable computational framework that couples the lattice Boltzmann method with the immersed boundary method on a dynamically adaptive octree grid. A key algorithm is developed for the efficient parallel host-cell searching, which significantly accelerates the tracking of Lagrangian points on distributed unstructured grids. The accuracy and robustness of the code are rigorously validated against canonical benchmarks, including the flow induced by an oscillating cylinder and the sedimentation of a sphere. The framework is applied to the multiscale problem of bubble-particle collisions. In quiescent flow, the simulations accurately capture the hydrodynamic interception mechanism, reproducing the theoretical collision efficiency scaling law proportional to the square of the particle-to-bubble size ratio. Furthermore, the framework is applied to the simulation of fully resolved bubbles interacting with inertial point particles in homogeneous isotropic turbulence.
item.dc:creator: Linfeng Jiang, Enrico Calzavarini, Dominik Krug

item.title: On the Two-Dimensional Structure and Asymmetries of Ionic Liquid Electrospray Plumes
item.description: arXiv:2605.24129v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Vacuum electrosprays play important roles in electrospray propulsion, a type of spacecraft electric propulsion wherein charged ions or droplets are accelerated at high velocity to provide spacecraft thrust, and they also have important implications for surface etching and mass spectrometry. Here we present the first fully two-dimensional time-of-flight (TOF) mass spectrometry survey of a vacuum electrospray plume, generated by a tungsten needle externally-wetted with the ionic liquid 1-Ethyl-3-methylimidazolium tetrafluoroborate (EMI-BF$_4$). We find that the plume exhibits clear two-dimensional compositional variation, structure, and asymmetry, with heavy particles and energetic neutrals being more prevalent in the center and a ring-shaped distribution for the monomers (the lightest molecular ions) peaking at 10$^\circ$ off beam-axis with a relative minima in the center. Using a new spatial baseline characterization method, we find a population of energetic neutrals firing 3.4$^\circ$ off beam-axis. In particular, we find that by comparing different parts of the plume, the estimated propulsive efficiency from any one sampled point may vary by as much as a factor of 6. We also find that high mass droplets, which are often assumed as absent in many studies of externally-wetted needles, may carry away significant propellant mass at lower effective velocity and reveal a cone-jet mode of operation at 470 nA output current. We thus find that whole-plume compositional surveys may more accurately assess plume composition and propulsive efficiency, and a significant portion of the `missing mass' in electrospray propulsion sources presumed to be operating in the pure ion regime can be potentially explained by limited sampling of the spatially non-uniform ion plume.
item.dc:creator: Zach Ulibarri, Giuliana Hofheins, Sophia Gessman, Elaine Petro

item.title: Orientation Dynamics of Rigid Fibers in a Microfluidic Burgers-like Vortex
item.description: arXiv:2607.14298v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Fiber suspensions are common in biological and environmental flows and are widely used in industrial applications. Fiber transport and orientation dynamics are affected by interactions with the surrounding fluid and strongly depend on the nature of the flow. The complexity of realistic flows, which are often heterogeneous or time-dependent, hinders a full understanding of fiber dynamics. In this study, we combine microfluidic experiments, theory and numerical simulations to investigate the orientation dynamics of rigid neutrally buoyant fibers in a well-controlled model system, a streamwise stationary vortex at moderate Reynolds number. Despite the three-dimensional nature of the flow, the orientation dynamics are remarkably simple: the fiber orientation is accurately described by Jeffery equations coupled with the Burgers-vortex model over a large range of particle Reynolds number. We show that fibers undergo uniform precession about the vortex axis driven by fluid vorticity while simultaneously aligning with the latter due to strain in the vortex core. These two motions are decoupled, with the alignment timescale determined by the local strain rate and the fiber aspect ratio. Finite particle size and inertia induce weak deviations from the base flow streamlines while leaving the orientational dynamics largely unaffected. These results establish a simple framework for understanding the behavior of elongated particles in stretched vortex flows, which constitute key building blocks of turbulence.
item.dc:creator: Marine Aulnette, Mathis Coutadeur, Cl\'ement Bielinski, Blaise Delmotte, Anke Lindner

item.title: Wave scattering around a submerged vertical permeable breakwater
item.description: arXiv:2608.06089v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: An analytical solution for a wave velocity field scattered by a submerged permeable vertical plate-type breakwater under the linear monochromatic wave is obtained and the applications of the solution are presented. The water has an infinite depth, and the flow is assumed to be incompressible, inviscid, and irrotational, which leads to the two-dimensional potential wave theory. The permeable breakwater vertically occupies a finite interval beneath the water surface and the water flows through the breakwater. The porous boundary condition is linear, but it couples the normal velocity on the plate to the discontinuity in the velocity potential across it, so that the scattering problem does not reduce directly to a Riemann-Hilbert problem of standard form. This is resolved by a perturbation expansion in a small dimensionless parameter representing the permeability. The solution is expanded up to the first order: the leading order gives the wave scattered by the impermeable breakwater through a homogeneous Riemann-Hilbert problem, and the first-order term gives the correction for the permeability through a nonhomogeneous Riemann-Hilbert problem. The far-field amplitudes follow in closed form up to a single Cauchy principal-value integral. The effects of wavelength, breakwater length, and breakwater permeability conditions on the reflection and transmission coefficients are discussed in detail as an illustrative example of the application of the solution. An exact energy identity is also derived; it verifies the first-order solution and yields a closed-form energy-consistency bound $\varepsilon_{\max}(kb)$ on the perturbation parameter, beyond which the truncated expansion ceases to conserve energy. The hydrodynamic load on the plate is obtained to the same order, and the leading-order results are verified against the closed-form solution of Evans for the impermeable plate.
item.dc:creator: Jeongin Kim, Yong Sung Park

item.title: Lagrangian Dynamical Theory of the Velocity Gradient Tensor: Real Schur Form, Schur Frame, Characteristic Vorticity Modes, and Commutative Vorticity Operators
item.description: arXiv:2609.14034v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The present work proposes a novel Lagrangian dynamical theory for the velocity gradient tensor (VGT) $\bm{A}\equiv\bm{\nabla}\bm{u}$, formulated on the basis of its canonical real Schur form.... The proposed theory is expected to be useful for understanding the evolution dynamics of the VGT rotational invariants and intrinsic vorticity modes in a variety of vortical flows.
item.dc:creator: Tao Chen

item.title: Directional Control of Droplet Motion via Geometric Gating
item.description: arXiv:2609.38654v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We explore new methods for inducing the movement of water droplets on elastomeric substrates, such as polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS). Our approach builds upon the well-known phenomenon that water droplets move easily across these substrates when swelled w,ith silicone oil. While designing shallow open channels and traps on a PDMS film offers a simple way to control a droplet's trajectory by tilting the substrate in two orthogonal directions, this method is poorly suited for manipulating multiple droplets simultaneously. To address this limitation, we introduce two new methods. The first method utilizes a plano-concave PDMS platform with a radius of curvature significantly larger than the size of the droplet and its translation distance. When the system's configuration is altered, this curved substrate consistently guides the droplet along a curved geodesic. The second method incorporates diode-like gates on the PDMS. These gates are created on either flat or plano-concave PDMS films by embedding thin, rigid plates into the elastomer prior to crosslinking, followed by swelling in silicone oil. This process generates sigmoidal steps that restrict droplet motion to a single direction. Finally, we demonstrate how combining these two strategies enables various forms of directed motion for both single and multiple droplets.
item.dc:creator: Manoj K. Chaudhury, Vanessa Elias, Michelle Fruge

item.title: Extension of a mathematical analogy between vortical flows without surface tension and irrotational capillary flows
item.description: arXiv:2610.10146v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In a recent paper, a mathematical analogy was found between two physically distinct classes of two-dimensional free boundary problems in inviscid fluid mechanics. One class involves free surface flows with constant vorticity in the bulk but without boundary surface tension, the other comprises free surface flows without vorticity in the bulk but with non-zero boundary surface tension (capillarity). Several examples were given of pairs of physically-distinct free boundary problems that amount to solving the same mathematical problem, albeit with the possibility of a single constraint arising for the capillary flows. The present work shows that this analogy extends to another pair of physically-distinct problems: a hollow vortex equilibrium in a shear flow with a third order irrotational strain and a steady bubble with surface tension in a simple straining flow. For both problems, we construct an isolated exact solution when a parameter $\gamma=0$ and provide numerical solutions for non-zero $\gamma$. An interesting feature is that non-trivial conformal mapping identities emerge from the class of problems with capillarity that apply equally for the hollow vortex problems when the parameters are appropriately constrained.
item.dc:creator: Valentin D. Kunz, Saleh Tanveer, Darren G. Crowdy

item.title: IGA-LBM: Isogeometric lattice Boltzmann method
item.description: arXiv:2509.11427v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The lattice Boltzmann method (LBM) offers intrinsic parallelism and simple boundary treatment, but Cartesian lattices approximate curved boundaries by stair steps, causing spurious forces and boundary-layer errors. We present an isogeometric collocation lattice Boltzmann method (IGA-LBM) that solves the discrete-velocity BGK system in strong form on body-fitted B-spline and NURBS geometries. Distribution functions are collocated at Greville points, advection is evaluated with high-order operators on the exact spline mapping, and time integration uses a four-stage Runge-Kutta scheme. Exact geometric metrics preserve a uniform free stream to machine precision on curved grids while retaining formal accuracy. The analysis recovers the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations with viscosity nu = cs^2 tau and shows that the main isogeometric advantage is exact geometry rather than a new interior stencil. Centered collocation is stabilized by a high-order filter, a physical-node closure restores fourth-order accuracy near clustered walls, and stiff collision limits the explicit step to dt <= 2.785 tau, scaling as O(Re^-1). Tests confirm the predicted accuracy and the O(Ma^2) compressibility floor. Validation covers the Ghia lid-driven cavity, steady and unsteady flow past a circular cylinder, and a body-fitted NACA0012 airfoil. For the cylinder, recirculation length is within about 9 percent and the Strouhal number within about 2.5 percent of reference values; drag is 6-12 percent above consensus and decreases with refinement, with stable wakes up to Re = 1000. For NACA0012 at Re = 500 and 10 degrees incidence, surface pressure and skin friction agree with reference data within a few percent. The method provides a high-order, free-stream-preserving LBM for curved-boundary flows based on exact B-spline and NURBS geometry, with demonstrated accuracy, stability, and geometric fidelity.
item.dc:creator: Ye Ji, Monica L\u{a}c\u{a}tu\c{s}, Matthias M\"oller

item.title: Chemical transport by weakly nonlinear internal gravity waves in stars
item.description: arXiv:2510.02031v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: While internal gravity waves (IGWs) are known to transport chemicals in the radiative zones of stars, substantial uncertainty remains regarding the magnitude and physical mechanisms of this transport. Most previous studies have relied on heuristic theories or numerical simulations that are difficult to extrapolate to stellar parameters. In this work, we present the first rigorous asymptotic calculation of (passive) chemical transport by IGWs, in the limit of small wave amplitude. The net vertical transport induced by a coherent packet of waves is found to be proportional to the horizontal mean of $(w^S+w^E)^2$, where $w^S$ and $w^E$ are the vertical Stokes and Eulerian mean velocities. The transport scales as the fourth power of wave amplitude and quadratically with time, and we verify these scalings with numerical simulations. In the weakly damped regime, the dominant transport coefficients scale as $\omega^{-2}\kappa^2$, where $\omega$ is the wave frequency and $\kappa$ is the radiative diffusivity. Because the transport can be positive or negative depending on the wave phases, the effective mixing induced by the superposition of coherent wave packets is expected to scale with the eighth power of wave amplitude. These results provide a theoretical foundation for making accurate predictions of IGW-induced chemical transport in stellar evolution models.
item.dc:creator: Yifeng Mao, Daniel Lecoanet

item.title: Chapman-Enskog expansion for chirally colliding disks
item.description: arXiv:2602.21367v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study a two-dimensional gas of hard disks undergoing chiral, energy- and momentum-conserving collisions. We propose a simple chiral collision rule and show that it can effectively capture collisions of spinning noncircular particles without retaining spin or orientation as kinetic variables. Despite the microscopic breaking of time-reversal symmetry, the H-theorem is obeyed, guaranteeing relaxation towards equilibrium in the absence of external forces. A Chapman-Enskog expansion yields analytical expressions for the shear and odd viscosity and the thermal conductivity. Theoretical predictions are confirmed by nonequilibrium molecular dynamics simulations
item.dc:creator: Ruben Lier, Pawe{\l} Matus
